Lesson 3 Overview
Renewable energy project financing is a cornerstone of the global energy transition.
<strong>Unlike fossil fuel projects, renewable energy initiatives typically involve high upfront capital costs but low operating and maintenance costs.
This unique financial profile requires tailored financing strategies that can mobilise investment, manage risk, and ensure long-term sustainability.
Governments, private investors, development finance institutions (DFIs), and communities each play a role in shaping the financial and delivery frameworks that make renewable energy projects viable.
This lesson introduces the core financing structures, sources of capital, and delivery models used in the development and deployment of renewable energy projects around the world.
M5: Derisking Renewable Energy Investment (DREI)
A: Introduction to Project Financing

The world has significant decarbonisation targets to reach by 2050, and the energy transition is estimated by Bloomberg and McKinsey to cost about $200 trillion.

Project finance brings together the stakeholders and components that make capital-intensive renewable energy projects a reality.

The basic premise of project finance is that lenders loan money for the development of a project solely based on the specific project’s risks and future cash flows.

As such, project finance is a method of financing in which the lenders to a project have either no recourse or only limited recourse to the parent company that develops or “sponsors” the project.

With so much money required and being earmarked to propel this transition, it is worth understanding how energy projects source funding, what goes into the “valuation” and risk assessments of these projects, as well as the parties and structures involved.

Project financing for renewable energy involves raising capital to develop, construct, and operate renewable energy projects.

Project financing has been used in various ways for many years, but in the 1970s and 1980s it emerged as a leading approach to financing large infrastructure projects that might otherwise be too expensive or speculative for any one individual investor to carry on its corporate balance sheet.

Project financing has been particularly important to project development in emerging markets, with participants often relying on guarantees, long-term off-take or purchase agreements, or other contractual relationships with the host sovereign or its commercial appendages to ensure the long-term viability of individual projects.
These were typically backstopped by multilateral lending agencies that mitigated some of the “political” risks to which the project lenders (and, sometimes, equity investors) were exposed
Project Finance Key Stakeholders

Sponsor / Developer
The entity (or consortium) that originates and leads the project.
Sets up the SPV, secures permits/land, and contributes a portion of equity.
Project Company / Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV)
The on‐balance‐sheet legal entity created specifically for this project.
Holds all contracts (EPC, supply, O&M, offtake) and raises capital from equity and debt.
Isolates project risk from sponsors’ broader balance sheets.
Community Stakeholders
Local communities, landowners, consumer groups, or local governments.
Provide “social license to operate” and may supply land, local workforce, or community‐based co‐investment.
EPC Contractor
Responsible for Engineering, Procurement, and Construction under a fixed‐price, turn‐key contract.
Once construction is complete, hands over to the Operator.
Tech Provider / Supplier
Supplies major equipment (e.g., solar PV modules, inverters, turbines, batteries).
May also provide warranties, commissioning, and spare parts.
Operator
Performs day‐to‐day operations and maintenance (O&M) of the plant.
Ensures performance standards, availability, and long‐term asset health.

Offtaker
The buyer of all (or part) of the project’s electricity output—commonly a utility or large corporate.
Offtake agreement (e.g., Power Purchase Agreement, or PPA) provides revenue certainty needed for debt repayment.
Regulators
National and local regulators set tariffs, licensing requirements, grid‐connection codes, and environmental approvals.
Regulatory stability is critical for project bankability and for lenders’ and investors’ risk assessment.
M5: Derisking Renewable Energy Investment (DREI)
B: Private investment financing elements – equity, debt, subsidies and variations of these concepts.
In a Build-Own-Operate (BOO) or similar private-led model, sponsors take on full and risk for delivering a project from concept through operation.

The capital they raise from investors must cover construction costs, service debt during operation, while the project’s revenues must deliver sufficient returns to equity investors.

A carefully structured capital stack aligns each investor’s risk tolerance with their expected return, minimizes the overall cost of capital, and underpins project bankability.

In a project-financed renewable energy transaction, sponsors draw on three broad “families” of capital—equity, debt and concessional support—each with distinct characteristics, cost profiles and risk positions.

Equity
is the ownership capital that underwrites the project’s very existence.
Whether it comes from the developer’s own balance sheet, from private-equity or impact-investor funds, or even from community co-investors, equity sits at the bottom of the repayment structure.
If anything goes wrong, for example construction delays, tariff shortfalls or operational struggles, it is the equity investors that absorb the first losses.
In return for taking that risk, equity investors expect the highest returns.
Their commitment not only demonstrates confidence to lenders but also aligns their incentive to ensure the project succeeds over decades.

Within the equity tranche, it is important to distinguish between common equity and preferred equity:
Common equity typically bears the most risk but also holds the greatest potential for upside, receiving returns only after all other obligations have been met.
Preferred equity, by contrast, has a more senior claim on cash flows and may offer fixed or capped returns, making it less risky than common equity but with more limited upside.
This layered equity structure allows projects to attract a broader mix of investors with varying risk-return preferences.

Debt
typically provides the bulk of project financing but carries lower returns and more stringent repayment requirements.
Debt typically provides most of the financing for a project but offers lower returns and comes with stricter repayment conditions.
Senior debt—from commercial banks, development finance institutions, or green bond investors—often covers 50 to 66 percent of the total capital.
These lenders have first claim on the project’s cash flows and usually require financial safeguards and legal rights over project assets.

Subordinated or mezzanine debt fills in some of the remaining gap—usually another 10 to 20 percent of the capital—in exchange for a higher interest rate, reflecting its junior position in the repayment order.

Concessional Support
Additionally to this capital stack pictured here, concessional support such as grants, soft loans and guarantees sits beneath commercial capital to bridge the gap between a project’s intrinsic risk-return profile and the thresholds required by mainstream investors.
A one-time viability-gap grant can lift the internal rate of return into acceptable territory.

Production-based incentives pay a top-up for every kilowatt-hour generated, smoothing revenue uncertainty.

Political-risk or payment-default guarantees from multilateral agencies effectively cap downside exposure for lenders.

Donors can thus can secure the bankability that purely commercial structures might not achieve.

Together, these three forms of capital are essential for renewable energy projects. Understanding their distinct roles and relative costs is fundamental before turning to the mechanics of sizing and sequencing each tranche.
M5: Derisking Renewable Energy Investment (DREI)
C: Concepts of project financial appraisal

Understanding the financial viability of a renewable energy project requires a set of interconnected concepts that together help assess expected returns, risks, and long-term sustainability.

Financial appraisal is the process of analysing a project's expected costs and revenues over time in order to determine its attractiveness to investors and lenders.

The starting point is the concept of the time value of money.
A dollar received today is worth more than a dollar received in the future due to the potential to earn a return on that money.
This idea underpins the use of discounting in project finance.
The discount rate is used to convert future cash flows into present value terms in order to estimate a project’s “worth”, today.
The discount rate selected reflects the project's risk profile and the required return by investors.

If the project is considered riskier, a higher discount rate will be applied (see Link for further reading).

The cost of capital is a central input in these calculations.

It refers to the expected return required by those who provide capital to the project – equity and debt being the two main forms.

The cost of equity is the return that equity investors expect for taking on the project's residual risk.

Equity is often the first-loss capital and thus bears more risk, requiring a higher return.

The cost of debt is the interest rate charged by lenders.

This is typically lower than the cost of equity, as lenders are repaid before equity holders and may have collateral in the project assets.

The weighted average cost of capital (WACC) comes into play when assessing whether the project is financially viable.
One common metric to assess the financial viability of a project is the Net Present Value, or NPV.
It represents the difference between the present value of expected cash inflows and the present value of cash outflows.
A positive NPV suggests that the project is likely to generate value for investors.

The WACC constitutes the discount rate used to calculate the NPV (see Link for further reading).

Relatedly, the Internal Rate of Return, or IRR, is the discount rate at which the NPV becomes zero.
It gives a sense of the project’s expected return and is often compared to a hurdle rate set by investors (see Link for further reading).

To estimate these indicators, it is necessary to detail the cost structure and revenue model of the project.

Renewable energy projects typically involve high upfront investment costs, known as capital expenditures or CAPEX.

These include the cost of equipment, installation, engineering, permits, etc,.

Operating expenditures, or OPEX, refer to the recurring costs over the project's life, such as maintenance, insurance, staffing, and administration.

Revenue streams depend on the type of project.
Utility-scale projects may earn income from power purchase agreements with utilities.

Mini-grids and decentralized systems can generate revenue through direct sales to households and businesses, while other projects may benefit from feed-in tariffs or government-backed incentives.

Finally, since future cash flows are uncertain, financial appraisal should incorporate risk analysis.
Sensitivity analysis tests how the project’s performance changes with variations in key assumptions, such as electricity prices, demand, or fuel costs.
Scenario analysis considers multiple future states of the world.

Together, these tools help developers and investors understand the project’s robustness under different conditions and whether it remains financially viable in the face of uncertainty.

This integrated approach to financial appraisal helps stakeholders evaluate both the potential and the limitations of renewable energy projects.
It also forms the analytical backbone of risk allocation and financing decisions under the DREI framework.

KEY TAKEAWAYS
Renewable energy projects need specialized financing structures

Because these projects require high upfront capital but deliver stable long-term revenues, financing is often structured through project finance and Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) that isolate risk, allocate responsibilities, and align the interests of developers, investors, lenders, and regulators.
Balancing the capital stack is key to investment feasibility
Equity, debt, and concessional capital each serve distinct purposes in renewable energy financing, with different risk–return profiles.

Evaluating feasibility depends on financial appraisal tools such as NPV, IRR, and WACC, alongside careful assessment of CAPEX, OPEX, and revenue models like power purchase agreements (PPAs) or feed-in tariffs.
Risk analysis and enabling conditions underpin project success

Sensitivity and scenario analysis help investors understand how changes in assumptions could affect returns, while stable contractual arrangements and supportive regulatory frameworks are essential for attracting capital, especially in developing and emerging markets.
